name: Van Fortress and Eski Van
tr: Van Kalesi ve Eski Van Şehri
desc: A kilometre-long limestone ridge above the lake plain, cut by the Urartians from 800 BC with royal rock tombs, niches and a trilingual inscription of Xerxes set high in the cliff. On the south side the flattened old city lies in open grass: two roofless mosques, one leaning minaret, nothing else.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; there is no shade anywhere on the rock and the summer glare off the lake is fierce
tip: Go up the west end an hour before sunset, then come down the south stair into the empty old city, which almost nobody realises is a whole vanished town.
todo: Roofless old city below the south face
rev: Almost everyone rates the sunset view and the sense of scale; the complaints are unfenced drops, a steep stepped path with loose stone, and hardly any signage explaining what you are looking at.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 20 min northwest; city buses run to the base of the rock and taxis wait there

name: Akdamar Island
desc: A 10th-century Armenian church alone on an island in Lake Van, its sandstone walls wrapped in a continuous band of relief: Jonah going into the whale, David with his sling, vines and hares and lions circling the drum. Almond trees cover the rest of the island and the water around it is turquoise and soapy with soda.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; boats stop running in strong wind in any month
tip: Walk the loop path round to the island's back side where the gulls nest and nobody goes — most people photograph the west facade and get straight back on the boat.
wiki: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar
todo: Relief band on the outer walls
Loop path round the far shore
rev: The carvings are consistently called the finest Armenian sculpture in Türkiye, but outside July and August boats leave only when full, waits of an hour are normal, and summer weekends bring loud picnic groups.
entry: ≈₺350 (≈€8) for the church plus ≈₺150 (≈€3.50) return boat · Museum Pass Türkiye covers the church
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 45 km west along the lake to the Gevaş jetty by dolmuş or taxi, then 20 min by boat

name: Lake Van
desc: Türkiye's largest lake and one of the world's biggest soda lakes: 3,700 square kilometres of water alkaline enough to feel slippery and to wash wool without soap. Volcanoes ring it — Nemrut at the west end, Süphan to the north, Erek behind Van — and the basin sits at 1,650 m, so the light is hard and the horizon enormous.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; the shore roads stay open all year but the winter wind off the water is savage
tip: The best free swim is off the shingle at Edremit south of Van in the evening; the water is warmer than it looks and you come out feeling as if you have used soap.
todo: Swim in the soda water at Edremit
Drive the north shore to Adilcevaz
Sunset with Süphan across the water
rev: People are surprised how clean and empty the water is, then complain about litter on the beaches nearest the towns, the near-total absence of changing facilities, and a lake so big that circling it eats a whole day.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport for the east shore or Muş (MSR) for the west; a car is the only practical way to see more than one shore

name: Çavuştepe
desc: An Urartian citadel strung along a narrow ridge above the Gürpınar plain, built by Sarduri II around 750 BC. The temple platform still carries polished basalt blocks with cuneiform cut so cleanly it looks machined, and you can trace the rock-cut cistern, the palace drains and the king's stone toilet.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the ridge is bare, with no shade and no water on site
tip: Ask for the site guardian — one of the few people alive who reads Urartian cuneiform, and he will read the blocks aloud, because the information boards tell you almost nothing.
todo: Cuneiform blocks on the temple platform
Ridge view over the Gürpınar plain
rev: Visitors call the stonework startlingly precise for 2,700 years old, while noting the site is small, entirely exposed, and usually bundled with Hoşap into a half-day that feels rushed.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 35 km southeast on the Hakkari road; Van–Başkale dolmuşes pass the turning

name: Hoşap Castle
desc: A Kurdish beylik castle of 1643 piled onto a rock over the Hoşap stream, its gate tower carved with two lions and an inscription. Inside are the shells of a mosque, a hamam and a dungeon, and a stretch of the old mud-brick town wall still runs along the slope below the road.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; snow can close the Başkale road between December and March
tip: The keeper often unlocks the gate when he sees a car pull up, but do not rely on it out of season — call the Van museum first or you will be photographing it from the road.
todo: Mud-brick town wall below the road
rev: The silhouette from the road draws more praise than the interior, which several visitors describe as largely rubble, and the castle is sometimes locked despite the posted opening hours.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 60 km southeast on the Hakkari road; Van–Başkale minibuses stop in Güzelsu village

name: Muradiye Waterfall
desc: The Bendimahi river drops about twenty metres over a black basalt lip north of Van, wide enough that spray reaches the suspension footbridge strung across the pool. In late spring the snowmelt makes it loud and brown; by August it is a thin curtain over green rock with tea gardens on both banks.
season: May–Jun at full snowmelt; by late August the flow is thin and the picnic crowds heavy
tip: Cross the swaying footbridge to the far bank and walk ten minutes downstream — those pools are empty while the near side is packed with tea tables.
todo: Suspension bridge over the plunge pool
Quiet pools downstream on the far bank
Tea and fried fish above the falls
rev: Impressive in May and merely pleasant in August, with recurring complaints about litter, pushy parking attendants and the volume of weekend picnic music.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 80 km north on the Doğubayazıt road; Van–Muradiye minibuses stop at the turning

name: Van Breakfast Street
desc: A block of shops in central Van that serve nothing but breakfast: herb cheese threaded with wild garlic, murtuğa of flour and egg fried in butter, kavut, clotted cream with comb honey, olives, tomatoes and bread arriving until you tell them to stop. Two people can sit for two hours and not clear the table.
season: Year-round — the reliable Van pleasure when the weather ruins everything else
tip: Order for one person fewer than you are, since the spread is priced per head and nobody finishes it, and insist on otlu peynir made with sirmo rather than the mild factory version.
todo: Murtuğa straight out of the pan
rev: Widely called the best breakfast in the country, with two consistent complaints: the quantity is wasteful, and the street is now touristy enough that some places run on volume rather than care.
entry: About ₺500–700 (≈€11–16) per person for the full spread
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, 6 km out; the breakfast street is a short walk off Cumhuriyet Caddesi in the centre

name: Van Cat Research Centre
desc: The white cats with one blue eye and one amber are bred and studied at a university centre on the northern edge of Van, where about a hundred live in heated pens and a grass run. Keepers open the kitten house at set hours; the adults ignore you and use the shallow pool when it suits them.
season: Year-round; kittens are most numerous Apr–Jul
tip: Time your visit to the morning feeding and cleaning round when the pens are opened — outside those windows most of the cats are asleep behind glass and it is a dull twenty minutes.
todo: Odd-eyed adults in the outdoor run
rev: Families and cat people enjoy it and the staff are attentive, but several visitors describe the enclosures as small and clinical, and you cannot buy or take home a cat however hard you try.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 15 min north by taxi to the Yüzüncü Yıl University campus at Tuşba

name: Gevaş and the Halime Hatun Tomb
desc: The 1358 tomb of a Karakoyunlu princess stands in a field of Seljuk-era gravestones on the edge of Gevaş: a twelve-sided drum under a conical cap, carved with rope braids and rosettes. The stones around it lean at every angle, some two metres tall, most of them unread for centuries.
season: Apr–Oct; the field is mud and grey stone in winter
tip: It is 400 m uphill from the Akdamar boat jetty and free — go while your boat fills up instead of sitting in the car park cafe.
todo: Carved drum of the Halime Hatun tomb
Lake view from the graveyard slope
rev: Those who find it call it the quietest good thing on the south shore, while noting there is no signage at all, nobody on duty, and grass left long enough to swallow the smaller stones.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 45 km west on the south-shore road; every Akdamar dolmuş passes through Gevaş

name: Lake Erçek
desc: A shallow soda lake east of Van with no outlet, rimmed by mudflats that flamingos work through from spring to autumn. There is no development at all — a track, some reed beds, a few shepherds — and on a still morning the mountains double themselves in the water.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct for flamingos and waders; the edges freeze Dec–Feb
tip: Come at first light from the Van side and stay in the car as a hide; step out and the flamingos lift off to the far shore and the drive is wasted.
todo: Sunrise reflections from the west shore
rev: Birders rate it highly and usually have it to themselves; everyone else notes there is nothing there at all — no hide, no cafe, no toilet — and the shore track turns to glue after rain.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 35 km east on the Özalp road; you need your own car to reach the shore

name: Çarpanak Island
desc: An uninhabited island off the north-east shore of Lake Van, joined to the land by a sand spit when the water is low. On it stands the roofless Armenian church of the Ktuts monastery, its walls streaked white by the gulls that nest in thousands across the island every summer.
season: May–Jun and Sep for boats and nesting gulls; no service in winter
tip: Boats go from the Van marina and are bargained per hull, not per head — round up a group at the jetty or you pay for the whole boat yourself.
todo: Gull colony on the north shore
Walk the sand spit at low water
rev: People who make it describe an unusually empty, slightly eerie place; the recurring problems are no scheduled boat, cancellations for wind, and gull droppings over absolutely everything in nesting season.
entry: Free to land · boat hire ≈₺2,500 (≈€55) per boat return
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 25 km north to the Van marina or Amik; boats are arranged on the spot

name: Semiramis Canal
desc: A stone-lined channel cut by the Urartian king Menua around 800 BC to carry spring water more than fifty kilometres to his capital at Van. Much of it still runs, and blocks set into the retaining walls carry his cuneiform curse on anyone who claims the work as theirs. Farmers near Gürpınar irrigate from it today.
season: Apr–Jun when the channel is full and the fields either side are green
tip: The easiest marked stretch is near Edremit south of Van; look for the low inscribed block in the bank rather than the channel, which looks like any farm ditch until you know what it is.
todo: Inscribed Urartian blocks in the bank
Follow a stretch on foot through fields
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors are impressed that a 2,800-year-old canal is still working, while everyone else finds it visually underwhelming and almost impossible to locate without a local pointing.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 20–35 km south; a car and some patience are needed to find the marked stretches

name: Ayanis Fortress
desc: A hilltop Urartian fortress above the north-east shore of the lake, built by Rusa II in the 7th century BC and burnt within a generation, which is why so much survived. The temple cella keeps courses of polished stone inlaid with a cuneiform frieze, and the walls look straight down onto the water with Süphan opposite.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the track in is rough and the hill has no shade
tip: Ask in Ağartı village for the guardian before you climb — the fenced temple enclosure is often locked and the walk up is twenty minutes on a goat path.
todo: Lake and Süphan view from the ramparts
Excavation trenches on the north side
rev: Those who make the effort rate the masonry and the setting above Çavuştepe, but the access road is unsurfaced, there is no ticket office or signage, and the best finds have gone to the Van museum.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then 35 km north along the lake to Ağartı; you need a car and the last 3 km are dirt

name: Bahçesaray and the Karabet Pass
desc: The road from Van to Bahçesaray climbs to nearly 3,000 m over the Karabet pass in a long series of switchbacks, then drops into a walnut-shaded valley that spends five months a year cut off by snow. The village keeps its stone houses and its own dialect; the road is why anyone comes.
season: Late Jun–Sep only; the pass is closed by snow from roughly November to May
tip: Fill the tank in Van and start early — there is no fuel and effectively no signal after the Müküs turning, and the pass is single-lane gravel with the drop on your side.
todo: Walnut groves in the Müküs valley
rev: Drivers call it one of the great roads in the country and one of the most nerve-racking, with rockfall, no barriers, and a genuine chance of being turned back by weather even in September.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport, then about 110 km southwest; hire something with clearance and do not attempt it in a low saloon

name: Nemrut Crater Lake
desc: The caldera of a collapsed volcano above Tatvan, seven kilometres across, holding a cold blue lake at one end and a small warm one at the other where steam still leaks out of the rock. Birch and willow grow inside the rim, which you see almost nowhere else in this region.
season: Late Jun–Oct once the crater road clears; snow closes it Nov–May, when it becomes a ski-touring objective
tip: The warm lake on the eastern side is genuinely bathable in August and hardly anyone walks the extra kilometre to it from the main viewpoint.
todo: Rim viewpoint over the whole caldera
Swim in the warm eastern lake
Steam vents on the north shore
rev: Consistently the highlight of a Bitlis trip in summer, with complaints about the rough final climb, weekend picnic litter around the main lake, and a season that really is only three or four months long.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport then 150 km round the lake to Tatvan, or Muş (MSR) 100 km; from Tatvan it is a 15 km climb by taxi or 4x4

name: Ahlat Seljuk Cemetery
desc: Around eight thousand red tuff headstones stand in a meadow above the lake, the tallest over three metres, carved with rope braids, rosettes and Kufic script in the 12th and 13th centuries. They lean in every direction because the ground has shifted for eight hundred years. Domed tombs of the same stone stand nearby.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; green in spring, gold in autumn, under deep snow Dec–Mar
tip: Come in the last hour of daylight when low sun rakes across the carving — at midday the flat glare turns the whole field into grey slabs.
todo: Tallest carved stones in the north field
Ulu Kümbet and the Bayındır tomb
rev: Visitors find the scale genuinely strange and moving, though the site is often billed as a World Heritage Site when it is only on Türkiye's tentative list, and there is no shade, cafe or interpretation on the ground.
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) airport then 190 km round the north shore, or Muş (MSR) 120 km; Tatvan–Ahlat minibuses run hourly

name: Bitlis Castle and the Great Mosque
desc: Bitlis is built of black volcanic stone in a gorge so narrow that the road, the river and the town share the floor. The castle sits on a rock in the middle of it, and the Great Mosque below dates from 1126, with a squat minaret and a plain interior of the same dark stone.
season: May–Oct; the gorge is icy and grey from December to March
tip: Park at the bottom and walk the stepped alleys up the east flank instead of driving to the castle — the old stone houses and medreses on that slope are the reason to stop in Bitlis at all.
rev: People who stop describe an atmospheric and entirely untouristed town, and also a noisy through-road, heavy lorry traffic in the gorge, and several monuments locked or wrapped in scaffolding.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport then 80 km east, or Van (VAN) 160 km round the lake; Bitlis sits on the main Tatvan–Diyarbakır road

name: Kef Castle, Adilcevaz
desc: An Urartian fortress of Rusa II on a spur of Süphan above Adilcevaz, reached by a steep track through walnut orchards. Blocks from its palace carried the well-known relief of a god standing on a bull, and the rampart lines look down over the lake to Nemrut. The medieval Adilcevaz castle stands separately on the shore.
season: Jun–Sep; the track is impassable with snow or mud outside that window
tip: Take the orchard path up from the hamlet rather than the road drawn on maps, and go with someone local, because the ruins are unfenced and easy to walk straight past.
todo: Urartian rampart lines on the spur
Lake and Nemrut view from the top
Adilcevaz castle down on the shore
rev: Rewarding for anyone interested in Urartu, but reports agree there is nothing on site — no markers, no boards, the relief blocks are in museums — and the climb is far steeper than it looks from town.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport then 130 km northeast round the lake, or Van (VAN) 150 km; a car is essential for the last stretch

name: Bitlis Old Bazaar
desc: A run of stone shops and old hans along the stream in the gorge, still selling what Bitlis produces: strung tobacco leaf, dark comb honey off the Nemrut and Süphan slopes, sacks of walnuts, and büryan lamb lifted out of a pit at midday. Half the buildings are 19th-century cut stone with vaulted backs.
season: Sep–Nov after the honey and walnut harvests; Fridays are the busiest day
tip: Buy honey by the comb rather than the jar and taste before you commit — the mountain honey is the real thing and there is plenty of blended stuff sitting next to it.
todo: Comb honey from the Nemrut slopes
rev: Travellers like that it is a working market rather than a tourist one, but note that it is cramped, cash-only, impossible to park near, and that most stalls shut early through the winter.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 80 km east; the bazaar lines the main road through the gorge in the town centre

name: Lake Van Train Ferry
desc: A working railway ferry crosses the lake between Tatvan and Van, rolling the wagons of the Tehran train onto its deck and taking around four hours. Foot passengers ride too, for very little money. Halfway across you lose sight of both shores and the volcanoes stand alone above the water.
season: Year-round, but sailings are weather-dependent and the timetable shifts constantly
tip: Departures follow the train, not a public schedule — ask at Tatvan station the day before, and bring your own food because the on-board buffet cannot be relied on.
todo: Watch the rail wagons roll aboard
Deck view of Nemrut and Süphan
Cross with the Van Gölü Ekspresi
rev: Rail travellers rate it one of the odder crossings anywhere, while warning about long waits at the pier, an unpredictable schedule and a plain, cold boat in winter.
entry: A few lira for foot passengers — buy at the pier
onward: Van Ferit Melen (VAN) or Muş (MSR) airports; the piers are at Tatvan İskele and Van İskele, both on the rail line

name: Mount Süphan
desc: Türkiye's second-highest volcano at 4,058 m, a broad snow cone standing alone over the north shore of Lake Van. The normal route from Aydınlar village is a long scree slog rather than a climb, with a crater lake near the summit that stays frozen into July and a view of Ararat on a clear day.
season: Jul–Sep for the summit; snow lingers on the upper cone until late June
tip: Camp around 3,200 m and start at three in the morning — the scree is frozen solid then and far easier than the loose afternoon mush.
rev: Climbers describe a straightforward but relentless ascent with a superb summit view, and warn that there is no water on the mountain and that altitude trouble is common from starting low and going fast.
entry: Free · notify the local jandarma post before climbing
onward: Muş (MSR) airport then 130 km northeast to Adilcevaz, or Van (VAN) 150 km; a taxi runs up to the Aydınlar trailhead

name: Malazgirt
desc: The town where the Seljuks broke the Byzantine army in 1071 keeps a good stretch of black basalt wall and four gates from its medieval fortress. The battlefield itself has never been located precisely; what exists is a modern memorial complex on the plain north of town and a small museum in the centre.
season: May–Jun and Sep; the anniversary events fall in late August and fill the town
tip: Come for the basalt walls and the emptiness of the plain rather than the monument, and avoid the anniversary week unless you want a political rally rather than a ruin.
todo: The open plain north of town
rev: Turkish visitors come for the history and are usually moved; foreign visitors more often report that there is very little to look at, that the memorial is modern and empty, and that the battle site is unmarked because nobody knows where it was.
entry: Free · small fee at the museum
onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 90 km northeast; Muş–Malazgirt minibuses run through the day

name: Muş Plain Tulips
desc: For about three weeks in spring the slopes above the Muş plain turn red with wild tulips — small, sharp-petalled, growing straight out of grazing land rather than beds. Families drive out at weekends to sit among them, and the fields move year to year with the grazing, so you ask rather than navigate.
season: Late Apr to mid-May only, and the exact fortnight shifts with the winter
tip: Ask at the tea houses in Kepenek or on the Bulanık road which slope is flowering that week — there are no signposts and last year's field is often bare.
todo: Red tulip slopes above the plain
rev: Those who time it right call it one of the best spring sights in the east; the common disappointment is arriving a week late to green fields, and grazing and picking thin the display every year.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 20–40 km out on the Bulanık or Malazgirt roads; you need a car and local directions

name: Lake Haçlı
desc: A shallow freshwater lake on the plain near Bulanık, spring-fed and rimmed with reeds. It is a breeding site for pelicans, grebes and marbled duck, and in early summer the open water is thick with them. There is nothing here beyond a track and a couple of fishermen's huts.
season: Apr–Jun for breeding birds; frozen and bleak Dec–Feb
tip: Take the north shore track for the birds; the south side is fished hard and the flocks stay well away from it.
todo: Reed beds on the north shore
rev: Birders rate the species list, but everyone notes the complete absence of facilities — no hide, no shade, no toilet — and that grazing and reed cutting have visibly thinned the cover in recent years.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 55 km northeast past Bulanık; your own car is needed for the shore tracks

name: Aslanlı Han
desc: A Seljuk-era han in the middle of Muş whose vaulted stone hall now shelters the small Hacı Şeref mosque. The masonry is heavy and plain, the arches spring low from the floor, and the building is wedged so tightly between shops that most people walk past the door without noticing it.
season: Year-round; the interior is cool in summer and freezing in winter
tip: Go in from the alley behind the shop row rather than the main street, and take your shoes off, because this is a working mosque and not a monument.
todo: Old stone houses on the slope above
rev: A five-minute stop that surprises the people who find it, though reports note poor signposting, doors locked outside prayer times, and an interior heavily altered by the mosque fitted into it.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 15 min into the centre; the han is a short walk from the main square

name: Muş Old Town and Castle
desc: The old quarter climbs the hill behind modern Muş in terraces of cut stone houses, with ruined castle walls on the crest and the 18th-century Alaeddin Bey mosque halfway up. From the top the whole plain opens out, flat to the horizon, with the Bingöl mountains white on the far side.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plain bakes in July and the hill is snowbound in winter
tip: Walk up late in the afternoon and come down through the Kale mahallesi alleys, where the houses still have carved lintels — a few more are lost to concrete every year.
todo: Carved lintels in the old alleys
rev: Visitors like the view and the feeling of an unvisited provincial town, while pointing out that the castle is little more than foundations, the climb is steep, and much of the old fabric is derelict.
onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 20 min into town; the old quarter begins directly behind the main street

name: Cilo Mountains and the Cilo Glacier
desc: A wall of limestone above Hakkari rising to Reşko at 4,135 m, carrying the largest glacier left in Türkiye under the summit ridge. The approach from Yüksekova crosses high pasture where Kurdish herders still spend the summer, then breaks into moraine, ice-scoured slabs and a milky glacial lake.
season: Jul–Sep only; snow lies on the approaches into July and weather closes in fast from mid-September
tip: Go with a Hakkari or Yüksekova guide and register at the jandarma post — this is a national park and also a sensitive border zone, and independent walkers are regularly turned back.
rev: Trekkers call it the most alpine landscape in the country, with heavy caveats: security checks and short-notice closures, no rescue infrastructure, and a vehicle festival that drove crowds onto the ice in 2024 and drew serious criticism from glaciologists.
entry: Free · a guide and jandarma notification are effectively required
onward: Hakkari Yüksekova (YKO) airport, then a 4x4 transfer to the trailheads; most people join an organised trek out of Van or Hakkari

name: Sat Lakes
desc: A scatter of glacial lakes at around 3,000 m in the Sat range, cupped in bare rock and fed by old snow, the deepest of them a hard blue that goes black under cloud. Reaching them means a long walk or a punishing 4x4 track; the reward is silence and no infrastructure of any kind.
season: Late Jul–Sep; snow blocks the approach for the rest of the year
tip: Do not try this as a day trip from Hakkari — the driving alone eats the daylight, and the shepherds' camps are the only shelter if the weather turns.
rev: The few trekkers who go rate it among the finest wild camping in Türkiye, but access depends on the security situation that month, the track destroys vehicles, and there is no signal and no rescue cover.
entry: Free · check current access with the jandarma before setting out
onward: Hakkari Yüksekova (YKO) airport, then 4x4 from Yüksekova; go with a local driver who knows the checkpoints

name: Zap Valley
desc: The Great Zab cuts a green gorge south from Hakkari toward the Iraqi border, with the road running on a ledge above it and the river turquoise in spring, jade by late summer. Rafting operators work the fast section below Hakkari; the rest is villages, poplars and long unlit tunnels.
season: May–Jun for high water and green slopes; the road is open all year but winter is grim
tip: Eat at the roadside tandır and fish places on the Çukurca side rather than in Hakkari town, and keep your ID in your hand, because there are several checkpoints on this stretch.
todo: Raft the fast section below town
rev: The scenery draws strong praise from the few who drive it, alongside honest reports of frequent military checkpoints, long roadworks, and government travel advisories that keep most foreign insurers out of the province.
onward: Hakkari Yüksekova (YKO) airport, then 70 km west to Hakkari; the valley road continues south toward Çukurca

name: Berçelan Plateau
desc: A wide grass plateau at about 2,500 m directly above Hakkari town, reached in half an hour of hairpins. In summer it fills with herders' tents, horses and families cooking on open fires, and the flat top is one of the few places in this province where you can simply walk without a border in the way.
season: Jun–Sep for the pastures; deep snow and a small ski lift in winter
tip: Weekday mornings you will have it to yourself; on Sunday it becomes the whole town's picnic ground, and the last stretch of road is rutted enough to want clearance.
rev: Locals rate it highly and visitors find the openness a relief after the gorges, though the plateau is heavily grazed, litter builds up through the summer, and access has been restricted at short notice in the past.
onward: Hakkari Yüksekova (YKO) airport, then 70 km to Hakkari and a 12 km climb by taxi or your own car

name: Meydan Medresesi, Hakkari
desc: A squat stone medrese of the 1700s in the middle of Hakkari, built under the Kurdish emirs who governed this country before Ottoman rule reached it properly. Restored a few years ago, it now houses the town museum, with local kilims, Kurdish and Nestorian material and photographs of the valleys before there were roads.
season: Year-round; effectively the only indoor sight in town and useful in bad weather
tip: Ask the curator about the Hakkari stelae — the Bronze Age warrior slabs found here are displayed in Van, and the story of how they turned up beats most of the labels.
rev: Small, nearly free, and better presented than people expect after the restoration, though several visitors found it shut without notice and the labelling is Turkish only.
entry: Free or a token fee — check locally
onward: Hakkari Yüksekova (YKO) airport, then 70 km west; the medrese is central, a short walk from the main square

name: Munzur Valley National Park
desc: Türkiye's largest national park on paper: about 42,000 hectares of limestone gorge, black pine and clear river between Tunceli and Ovacık. The Munzur runs green over white stone the whole way, with wild goats on the crags and trout in the pools, and the road beside it is one long series of places to stop.
season: May–Oct; the high country holds snow into June and the road can be cut in winter
tip: The stretch above Ovacık is the wild part — most visitors stop at the first picnic spots ten minutes out of Tunceli and never see the gorge proper.
todo: Drive the gorge road to Ovacık
Wild goats on the limestone crags
rev: Tunceli people call it the finest valley in the country and outsiders usually agree, but the park has fought hydroelectric schemes for two decades, side valleys are still closed for military operations at times, and facilities are basic.
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport then 130 km north to Tunceli, or Erzincan (ERC) 180 km; the park road starts at the edge of town

name: Ovacık and the Munzur Pastures
desc: Ovacık sits at 1,300 m in a bowl of high pasture under the Munzur range, with snow on the tops into July and thick honey coming off the meadows in August. The town itself is small and plain; the reason to come is the road beyond it toward the Munzur springs and the empty valleys on either side.
season: Jun–Sep for the pastures; the district is snowbound and half-empty Dec–Mar
tip: Buy Ovacık honey from a producer in the villages rather than a shop on the main road, and expect to be fed while you negotiate.
todo: Snow on the Munzur tops in July
rev: Visitors describe real hospitality and empty landscapes; the practical warnings are very limited accommodation, occasional road closures for military operations, and almost nothing open outside summer.
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 130 km to Tunceli and 60 km further up the valley; minibuses run from Tunceli otogar

name: Munzur Springs
desc: The Munzur comes out of the base of a mountain wall above Ovacık in a line of springs, full-sized from the first metre, ice cold and clear enough to read through. The site is sacred to local Alevis, who tie cloth to the trees and bring food, and there are tea tables in the shade beside the water.
season: Jun–Sep; the road up is often blocked by snow outside that
tip: This is a place of worship as much as a picnic ground — do not put beer on the table, and ask before photographing anyone at the water.
todo: Springs bursting from the rock wall
Cloth tied to the shrine trees
Trout and tea under the poplars
rev: People find it genuinely beautiful and unusually charged with meaning; the complaints are weekend crowds, music from the picnic areas, and litter left around the pools by day-trippers.
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 130 km to Tunceli, 60 km to Ovacık and 10 km more to the springs by car or village dolmuş

name: Pertek Castle
desc: A Seljuk-era castle that used to stand on a hill and now stands on an island, after the Keban reservoir flooded the valley around it in the 1970s. Walls and towers rise straight out of the water, and the small car ferry between the Elazığ and Tunceli banks passes close enough to photograph it from the deck.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the reservoir is at its lowest and least attractive in late summer
tip: You do not need to land — take the Pertek car ferry across the reservoir and you get the castle from the water plus the crossing itself for the price of a ticket.
todo: Castle rising straight out of the reservoir
Sultan Hatun mosque in the town
rev: The setting is what people remember; the interior gets far less praise, landings depend on the water level and a willing boatman, and the ferry timetable is loose at the best of times.
entry: Free from the water · small fee if a boatman lands you
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 60 km north to the Pertek ferry pier; the crossing drops you on the Tunceli road

name: Halvori Springs
desc: Twenty kilometres up the Munzur gorge from Tunceli, cold springs come out of the canyon foot straight into the river under willows, with wooden platforms built out over the water. People swim in the green pools, eat trout, and sit in the spray on the platforms all afternoon.
season: Jun–Sep; the water is too cold and the road too rough outside summer
tip: Swim upstream of the platforms rather than below them — those pools are deeper, colder and free of the frying-oil sheen off the restaurants.
todo: Canyon walls seen from the water
rev: A local favourite and cheap, though visitors mention rubbish along the bank at weekends, loud music from the restaurants, and river water cold enough to cramp your legs within a minute.
entry: Free · platforms and meals charged by the restaurants
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 130 km to Tunceli and 20 km up the Ovacık road; summer dolmuşes run from Tunceli otogar

name: Pülümür Valley
desc: The road from Erzincan down to Tunceli threads a red and ochre gorge for sixty kilometres, following the Pülümür stream past terraced hamlets and single-arch bridges. In late October the poplars along it turn yellow the whole length, and outside the summer months there is almost no traffic.
season: May–Oct; the pass at the Erzincan end closes with snow in winter
tip: Drive it north to south in the afternoon so the light is on the red rock, and stop in Pülümür town for trout, because there is nowhere else to eat on the entire road.
rev: Drivers rate it among the best roads in the east; the honest notes are rockfall after rain, sparse fuel, and long stretches with no signal and no settlement.
onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then south on the Tunceli road; Elazığ (EZS) works from the other end via Tunceli

name: Bingöl Floating Islands
desc: On a small lake in the hills above Solhan, mats of peat and root have broken free of the shore and drift with the wind, carrying grass and flowers with them. They are a registered natural monument, a few metres across, and they visibly change position over the course of a day.
season: May–Sep; the lake freezes and the track is poor in winter
tip: Go on a day with a light breeze — in dead calm the islands do not move at all, which is the entire point of the trip.
todo: Watch an island drift across the lake
rev: A genuinely odd natural phenomenon that people enjoy once they get there, with consistent complaints that the lake is small, the last kilometres are dirt track, and signposting from the main road is poor.
onward: Bingöl (BGG) airport, then 60 km east to Solhan and a short climb on a rough track; a car is needed

name: Kral Kızı Castle
desc: A ruined fortress on a 1,400 m spur outside Genç, wrapped on three sides by streams so that only the eastern approach is walkable. What survives is broken wall lines and rubble rather than standing towers, and the local story gives it to a Persian king who shut his daughter away up there.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; scrub and snakes in high summer, mud in winter
tip: Treat it as a walk with a view rather than a monument — the spur above the stream junction is the real reward, and there is no path, so wear boots.
todo: Surviving wall lines in the scrub
rev: Honestly more legend than ruin — no signage, no path and little masonry left standing — but people who like empty hills and a good story find it worth an afternoon.
onward: Bingöl (BGG) airport, then 35 km south to Genç, then about 3 km on foot or by farm track

name: Battalgazi (Old Malatya)
desc: Old Malatya was abandoned for the new town in the 19th century, so what remains sits among apricot orchards: a long circuit of brick and stone city wall with round towers, the 1224 Great Mosque with a blue-tiled Seljuk iwan, and the huge Silahtar Mustafa Paşa caravanserai.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; blossom in early April, 40 °C in the July orchards
tip: The tiled iwan of the Ulu Cami is behind a locked courtyard door much of the time — turn up at prayer time and find the muezzin rather than coming mid-morning.
todo: Tiled iwan of the Ulu Cami
Walk a stretch of the city wall
rev: Visitors like that a whole medieval town survives among the orchards, while noting that the 2023 earthquakes damaged several buildings, restoration hoarding is widespread, and opening hours are unpredictable.
entry: Free · small fee at the han
onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 35 km northeast; city buses run out from Malatya through the day

name: Arslantepe Mound
desc: A thirty-metre mound above the Malatya plain, occupied from the sixth millennium BC, where excavators found the earliest known palace complex and a hoard of early arsenical bronze swords. A canopy now covers the mud-brick palace and its wall paintings, which is the only reason the walls are still standing.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plain reaches 40 °C in July and August with no shade on the mound
tip: Come in the morning, when low sun still shows the paint on the mud brick — under a midday sun the whole site flattens into beige.
todo: Lion gate stones and site museum
rev: Archaeologically extraordinary and quiet enough that you may have it alone, though visitors regularly say it looks like a building site unless you read the boards first, and the best finds are in the Malatya and Ankara museums.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 30 km east to Orduzu on the Battalgazi road; a taxi from Malatya takes 20 min

name: Levent Valley
desc: A canyon cut into pale rock north of Akçadağ, with walls up to 200 m, a village of the same name on the rim, and rock-cut tombs and pigeon houses in the cliffs. Bolted sport-climbing routes have gone up on the best walls, and a path runs along the floor when the stream is low.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; summer is too hot for the walls and the floor floods with the spring melt
tip: Ask in Levent village for the way down to the canyon floor — the rim viewpoints are what everyone photographs, but the rock-cut chambers are all down at the bottom.
rev: Climbers and walkers rate it well above its reputation, with the drawbacks being a rough approach road, no facilities in the village, and route information that circulates mostly by word of mouth.
onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 60 km west past Akçadağ; a car is essential and the final stretch is narrow

name: Malatya Apricots and the Sire Pazarı
desc: Malatya grows most of the world's dried apricots and nearly all of them pass through the Sire Pazarı, a covered hall where jute sacks are cut open, graded by hand and traded by shouting. In July the orchards are full of trays drying in the sun, and the unsulphured fruit comes out brown and tastes far better.
season: Jul–Aug for the harvest and the drying trays; the market trades all year
tip: Ask for kükürtsüz, the dark unsulphured fruit, and try the apricot kernels while you are there — the bright orange stuff is sulphured for export.
todo: Grading floor at the Sire Pazarı
rev: Food travellers rate the market as the real thing rather than a display, though it is dusty, loud, hard to photograph without asking, and much of the city around it is still rebuilding after the 2023 earthquakes.
onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 30 min into the city; the Sire Pazarı is near the old centre and easy by taxi

name: Darende and the Tohma Canyon
desc: The Tohma cuts a narrow gorge through Darende, and a walkway is bolted to the rock a few metres above the water, running past the Somuncu Baba shrine complex and its pool of fat carp. Above the town the canyon opens out, with boat rides and a cable car that are pure Turkish weekend.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the shrine is busiest at weekends and religious holidays
tip: Walk the canyon boardwalk early, before the pilgrim coaches arrive and the whole gorge fills with people throwing bread at the fish.
todo: Somuncu Baba complex and carp pool
Boat trip in the upper gorge
rev: A genuinely pretty gorge with a well-made walkway, though the shrine end gets very crowded, the commercial add-ons feel bolted on, and parking in the town is chaos on Sundays.
entry: Free · boat and cable car charged separately
onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 100 km west on the Kayseri road; Malatya–Darende buses run several times a day

name: Günpınar Waterfall
desc: Spring water emerges from the hillside above Darende and falls in a broad fan of small cascades over travertine steps into a wooded basin, with tea tables built into the terraces. It runs at much the same volume all year, which is unusual here, and the water stays cold through August.
season: May–Oct; the terraces ice over and the access road gets slippery in winter
tip: Walk up past the last tea table to the head of the falls where the springs actually come out — most people stop at the first platform and photograph the same view as everyone else.
todo: Springs at the head of the falls
rev: Praised as cool, green and cheap in a very hot province, with complaints about litter and loud music on summer weekends and a final access road that is narrow and badly surfaced.
onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 110 km west via Darende; a car is needed for the last 12 km

name: Harput
desc: The old town of Elazığ sits on a rock plateau three hundred metres above it, half-abandoned when the population moved down in the 19th century. What is left is a big Artuqid-era castle, the 1156 Great Mosque with a leaning brick minaret, the Meryem Ana church, and a view across the plain to Hazar lake.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plateau is windy and cold from November onward
tip: Go up in the evening for kürsübaşı music and orcik sweets at the cafes below the castle — daytime is coach parties, and the castle interior has been largely closed since the earthquakes.
todo: Castle rock and the plain view
Leaning minaret of the Ulu Cami
rev: Visitors rate the setting and the mosque highly, but note that the castle has been closed or half-closed for restoration for years, several churches are locked, and the plateau is bleak in wind.
entry: Free · small fee at the castle when it is open
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 15 km north up the escarpment; city buses and taxis run up from the centre

name: Lake Hazar and the Sunken City
desc: A deep blue lake at 1,250 m in a trough of the East Anatolian Fault, with the walls of a drowned medieval settlement lying a few metres under the surface near the southern shore. When the water drops in late summer the tops of the walls break the surface and you can wade out to them.
season: Jul–Sep for swimming and the lowest water; windy and cold the rest of the year
tip: The ruins show best in September after the drawdown; dive clubs in Sivrice run trips over them, and from the shore you need a mask to see anything at all.
todo: Wade or dive to the sunken walls
rev: People are surprised how clear and cold the water is; the complaints are shoreline development at the Sivrice end, an underwhelming sunken city unless the level is low, and a strong wind most afternoons.
entry: Free · dive trips charged by the club
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 30 km southeast on the Diyarbakır road to Sivrice; minibuses run from Elazığ otogar

name: Keban Dam
desc: The first of the big Euphrates dams, finished in the mid-1970s: a two-hundred-metre wall across a gorge that backed up a reservoir the size of a small sea. It drowned villages and the whole valley floor, and created the water that Pertek castle now stands in. The viewpoint above the crest looks down the length of the gorge.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the reservoir shore is dusty and low by late summer
tip: Photographing the dam structure is restricted — shoot from the public viewpoint on the road above and keep the lens off the installations and the guard posts.
rev: Engineering interest and sheer scale are the draw; visitors warn that access to the dam itself is controlled, security is touchy about cameras, and nothing at all is organised for tourists on site.
entry: Free · no public access to the structure
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 60 km northwest to Keban town; the viewpoints are on the road above the dam

name: Buzluk Cave
desc: A limestone cave north of Harput that does everything backwards: it fills with ice through the summer and thaws in winter, because cold air sinks into the shaft and cannot get out again. In August there are ice columns on the floor while the hillside outside sits at 35 °C. Steps lead down about thirty metres.
season: Jul–Aug for maximum ice, which is the opposite of what you would expect
tip: Take a torch and a jacket — there is no lighting, the steps are wet, and the temperature drops thirty degrees in the first minute of the descent.
todo: Summer ice columns on the cave floor
rev: A memorable ten minutes and a real curiosity, but reports agree the access road is rough, the entrance is unsigned and sometimes gated, and there is no lighting or handrail inside.
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then about 25 km north beyond Harput on a minor road; a car and local directions are needed

name: Palu
desc: Old Palu stands abandoned on a cliff above the Murat river: an Urartian citadel with a cuneiform inscription of King Menua, a ruined Ottoman mosque and hamam, and the shell of an Armenian church, all in the same brown stone. The modern town sits on the flat a kilometre away.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the cliff is exposed and July is brutally hot
tip: The Menua inscription is cut into the rock high on the citadel and is easy to walk past — look on the north face above the old cistern.
todo: Menua cuneiform on the citadel rock
Murat river view from the cliff edge
rev: Rewarding for anyone who likes ruins nobody else visits, though the climb is steep and unshaded, there is no signage, and the 2023 earthquakes brought down more of the standing walls.
onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 75 km east on the Bingöl road; Elazığ–Palu minibuses stop in the new town below
